lesson.menu_title: Cinema and Culture — Saying More Than That You Liked It

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- Cinema and Culture

phases: Words for What a Film Does
lesson.grammar_point: hedging language for degrees of certainty

listenings.text: Right, before we start arguing, the rule of this club, for anybody who is here for the first time. Any opinion is allowed. Any one at all. The only thing that is not allowed is saying that it was good and then stopping there, because that leaves the rest of us with nothing to answer. One reason, that is all I ask. Now, my own position, and you are free to take it apart. It strikes me that the ending is deliberately ambiguous, and I say that as somebody who usually hates being left in the dark. And a warning about the second half. It appears slow the first time you watch it, and two people I know walked out at exactly that point, which means they missed the thing the whole film had been building for ninety minutes.

Here is the only piece of advice I give people who tell me they cannot talk about films in English. There is nothing wrong with saying that a film was good. It is true, it is polite, and it is finished, and a finished sentence gives the other person absolutely nothing to answer. So use a formula instead. One hedge, one specific thing that is actually in the film, and one reason, in that order. It strikes me that the portrayal of the mother is the only honest thing in it, because she is the only one who never explains herself. That takes about six seconds and there is nothing clever about it. What it does is remarkable, though. People begin treating you as somebody worth talking to, and it has almost nothing to do with how good your English is.

extra_audio.text: Claire asks Braulio what the film did to him, two days after the screening. Braulio answers that it is a much smaller film than it pretends to be, and that he means it as a compliment. He argues that the war is only an undertone and that the real subject is the kitchen. Claire objects that there is a sense the director does not trust his audience, because he explains the last scene twice. Braulio concedes the point to some extent and says he would rather be explained to twice than told what to feel once.

reading.rtitle: Why Nobody in English Says That They Liked It
paras: There is a moment at every dinner where somebody asks what you thought of something, and the honest answer is short. You liked it. It was good. In Portuguese that answer can carry a whole opinion, because the tone and the face do the rest of the work. In English it carries almost nothing, and the conversation stops there, politely, and moves on to somebody else.

The reason is not vocabulary, and it is not confidence. It is that an English opinion is expected to arrive unfinished. It strikes me that the ending is deliberately ambiguous. One could argue that the portrayal of the mother is the only honest thing in the film. To some extent the whole genre is built on that single idea. Each of those is a firm opinion, stated by somebody who means it, and each of them hands the other person somewhere to go.

This catches people out in a way they do not expect. A speaker who is careful and precise in his own language often produces the flattest sentences in his second one, because the machinery he uses to be careful has not been translated yet. He knows exactly what he thinks about the tension in a film and the political undertone running under it, and what comes out of his mouth is that it was very good. The gap is not between what he thinks and what he knows. It is between what he thinks and what he has the tools to hand over.

The machinery itself is small. Five openings, and the habit of naming one specific thing rather than the whole film. It strikes me that, one could argue that, to some extent, there is a sense that, I tend to think that. None of them means the speaker is unsure, and anybody who reads them that way has misread the room. They mean the speaker is still talking, which is the only thing an English dinner table is really asking of anybody.
